correctness.rationale: All 1,253 graph-atlas representatives through seven vertices were reconstructed; an at-most-seven-vertex graph has matching-complex dimension at most two. Exact signed integral second boundaries yield Smith invariants for H1 torsion (the H0 boundary image is free). Forty classes have exactly one nonunit invariant 3; all are order seven and the unique 13-edge case is G1105. A 42×30 matrix for that case has Smith diagonal 29 ones plus one 3 and first boundary rank 12; a separate explicit integral chain certificate has ∂2 c=3z and ∂1 z=0, with ∂2 injective and c not divisible by 3, so z is nonzero of order 3. Independent complementary-line-graph clique enumeration and prime-field ranks reproduce the exact class list. No unenumerated simplices occur.

originality.rationale: Primary full-text comparisons distinguish the known 3-torsion of the complete-seven-vertex matching complex (21 graph edges) from the sharp 13-edge threshold and exhaustive 40-class census. The flag-complex torsion theorem covers at most twelve simplicial vertices, below the sparse witness’s thirteen, and the two-dimensional Buchsbaum matching-complex theorem classifies a distinct topological property. A full index and graph-alias literature search found no equivalent or stronger covering statement. Residual risks are recorded; this is not an assertion of absolute priority.
residual_risks: An equivalent edge-sparse matching-complex torsion census could exist in unindexed literature.
The Graph Atlas catalog is treated as a complete external enumeration of unlabeled graphs through order seven; its construction is not reproven.
Computational algebra software and independently implemented finite-field elimination are not a third-party mathematical audit.

value.rationale: The earliest possible graph order for 3-torsion in ordinary matching-complex H1, together with its exact edge-density threshold within that order, unique sparsest seven-vertex witness and all forty order-seven torsion types, addresses a natural boundary of the complete-graph torsion phenomenon. The 13-edge threshold is mathematically motivated by minimality, not an arbitrary graph slice. Complete finite classification with a signed integral witness supplies a reusable benchmark for torsion under graph-edge deletion without requiring a general graph-family theorem.
